titre: Skulls Sent Home Before the Apology
accroche: Between 2011 and 2018, Germany returned to Namibia skulls collected during colonization. The official words of acknowledgment did not follow them.
contenu_vulgarise:
Between 1904 and 1908, the German army waged a campaign in its colony of German South-West Africa, today Namibia, against the Herero and Nama peoples, who had risen up against the occupation. On October 2, 1904, General Lothar von Trotha signed an order that would go down in history as the “extermination order” (Vernichtungsbefehl), targeting Herero who remained in the territory; Kaiser Wilhelm II did not withdraw it until the following December 6. Survivors were interned in concentration camps, notably at Swakopmund and Lüderitz. Historians estimate that between forty thousand and eighty thousand Herero died during this period, about 80 percent of their pre-war population, and about ten thousand Nama, close to half of theirs.

## Skulls Sent to Germany for Science

Human remains of victims, skulls in particular, were sent to Germany: physicians and researchers saw in them material for the racial theories then flourishing, supposedly proving African inferiority scientifically. It was in that same colony that, in 1908, the German physical anthropologist Eugen Fischer conducted, drawing on Mendel's genetic theory, a study of three hundred and ten children born to Nama women and white men in Rehoboth. Published in 1913, it concluded that African blood was “impure”; the ban on mixed marriages, already in force in Namibia since 1905, was extended to all German colonies in 1912. Fischer became the first director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Anthropology in Berlin in 1927, where the young Josef Mengele would later spend time as a researcher, under the direction of Otmar von Verschuer, who succeeded Fischer in 1942.

## Skulls Returned, Words That Lagged Behind

A century later, German collections began returning these remains. Handovers took place in 2011 and 2014, then, on August 29, 2018, twenty-seven Herero and Nama human remains were returned at a ceremony in a Berlin church, followed by a second ceremony in the Namibian Parliament garden two days later. Germany had, however, already acknowledged in 2015 that the events of 1904-1908 could be called genocide. But at the August 2018 restitution ceremonies themselves, political scientists Reinhart Kössler and Henning Melber note an absence of formal recognition of the genocide, of any official apology, and of any mention of reparation. In Berlin, Minister of State Michelle Müntefering bowed in deep mourning and asked for forgiveness from the bottom of her heart, but those words, they judge, were not a deep apology from the state: she spoke of atrocities committed in Germany's name that would today be called a genocide. It was only in 2021 that Germany proposed an agreement providing 1.1 billion euros in development aid for Namibia, presented as an ex gratia gesture and without acknowledging legal responsibility; Herero and Nama representatives rejected it and continue to demand reparations.

The skulls thus traveled the reverse of what one would expect from acknowledgment: they came home without the German state offering, at the very moment of their return, any formal acknowledgment or official apology, and the financial aid proposed in 2021 acknowledged no legal responsibility. Returning a body, in this story, was not enough to return with it the admission of the wrong that had sent it on its journey.

repere.texte: On October 2, 1904, General Lothar von Trotha signed the “extermination order” targeting the Herero; Kaiser Wilhelm II did not withdraw it until the following December 6.

carte.punch: Herero and Nama skulls came home to Namibia without formal recognition of the genocide or an official apology.
carte.idee: Between 1904 and 1908, colonial Germany killed about 80 percent of the Herero and half the Nama in Namibia, and sent victims' skulls for racial research. Returned as early as 2011, remains were still being handed back in 2018 without formal acknowledgment or an official apology from the German state.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Full timeline of the 1904-1908 campaign, the concentration camps, and the stages of Germany's acknowledgment.

quiz.question: In August 2018, Germany returns twenty-seven Herero and Nama human remains at a ceremony in Berlin, followed by another in Namibia. What is missing from the German state's side, even though its Foreign Ministry had confirmed in 2015 that the word “genocide” could apply?
choix: Any formal recognition of the genocide, any official apology, and any mention of reparation
Any representative of Herero and Nama descendants in the Berlin church
Any German government official at the ceremony
Any actual handover of human remains to the Namibian delegations
quiz.explication: Although the German Foreign Ministry had confirmed as early as 2015 that the word “genocide” could apply, the August 2018 ceremonies include no formal recognition, no official apology, and no mention of reparation. Minister Müntefering asks for forgiveness there, but her words are judged far from a deep apology from the state; an aid agreement is not proposed until 2021.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does General Lothar von Trotha order on October 2, 1904?
choix: An immediate ceasefire with Herero and Nama chiefs
The complete withdrawal of German troops from the colony
An extermination order (Vernichtungsbefehl) targeting Herero who remained in the colonial territory
The creation of a protected farming reserve for the Herero
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On October 2, 1904, Trotha signs the order known as the Vernichtungsbefehl, targeting Herero who remained in the colonial territory; Kaiser Wilhelm II would not withdraw it until two months later, on December 6.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the study Eugen Fischer conducts in 1908 on 310 children born in Rehoboth conclude?
choix: That no measurable difference exists between the population groups studied
That mixed ancestry improves these children's resistance to tropical disease
That the racial theories current at the time lack any scientific foundation
An “impurity” of African blood, which weighs into the ban on mixed marriages extended to the German colonies in 1912
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Fischer concludes that the mixed-ancestry children he studies have “impure” blood; this conclusion, published in 1913, weighs into the 1912 extension to all German colonies of a ban on mixed marriages already in force in Namibia since 1905.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Germany accept in the agreement proposed to Namibia in 2021, and what does it refuse?
choix: It acknowledges full legal responsibility before an international tribunal
It proposes 1.1 billion euros in development aid, as an ex gratia gesture, without acknowledging legal responsibility
It returns all the colonial lands occupied by its nationals in Namibia
It pays direct individual reparations to every registered Herero and Nama family
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 2021 agreement provides 1.1 billion euros in development aid, presented as an ex gratia gesture and without acknowledging legal responsibility; Herero and Nama representatives reject it for that reason and continue to demand reparations.
